prize_parts.citation: For showing how productivity differences across firms determine who exports and invests abroad, and for reworking the theory of gains from trade around firm-level selection and reallocation.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B014 with Melitz and Helpman. I tightened the citation after the exchange so that it credits the selection-and-reallocation framework and not the broader firm-level trade literature. The discovery is one compact idea. Firms differ in productivity, only the more productive ones select into exporting and foreign investment, and trade therefore reallocates resources across firms within industries. Melitz (2003) is the pivotal model. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) extend it to exports versus FDI, which is the natural second credit. The framework produced sharp, testable predictions on exporter premia and firm sorting. These have been confronted with firm- and transaction-level data for over twenty years. It is now standard in teaching, in policy analysis, and in macro and IO applications. Two names carry the core without an arbitrary cut, so the three-name cap does not bind the way it does for B009. I treat the round-1 counts (seven for B009 split across two trios, three for B014) as information about attribution, not merit. B009 is very close on merit, and the choice between them rests on how cleanly each can be bounded in a citation.
statement.case_against: Attribution and priority remain the main weakness. Bernard and Jensen on exporter premia, Eaton and Kortum on quantitative Ricardian trade, and Hopenhayn on firm dynamics have strong claims to adjacent work and are not credited on this line. Krugman's 2008 prize covered earlier new trade theory, and Helpman's credit is also split with B049. Arkolakis, Costinot and Rodriguez-Clare show that headline welfare gains from selection depend on functional-form assumptions and may be smaller than first suggested. The citation therefore cannot claim a large aggregate welfare number. I also work on pricing under imperfect competition, pass-through and firm-level trade data. This is adjacent to the B014 literature and may make me value firm-level microfoundations more than colleagues from other fields would. I do not treat that familiarity as merit.

responses.point: Dreber Almenberg ranked B014 sixth. She weighs Krugman's 2008 prize, the uncredited priority claims of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and the contested size of welfare gains from selection more heavily than the framework's reach. She asked B014 supporters to say how they weigh these.
responses.response: I weigh the three points differently from one another. On Krugman 2008, I read that prize as recognising scale economies, product differentiation and trade patterns with representative firms. Melitz's object is different: productivity-sorted firms and endogenous selection into exporting. On welfare size, Arkolakis et al. show that aggregate gains can be summarised by few statistics under common restrictions. That qualifies the magnitude, but it does not remove the selection margin, which still matters for reallocation and distribution. It is also why I word the citation around selection and reallocation, not around gains of a given size. Priority is the point I cannot fully discharge. A citation limited to the selection model leaves the empirical exporter-premia facts and the Ricardian quantitative line uncredited, and I think that is defensible. But I cannot settle from the supplied evidence whether it fully answers Bernard-Jensen and Eaton-Kortum. I accept that this is a real cost and a legitimate reason for your ranking.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B009 first and B014 fourth. He accepts Melitz-Helpman as mature and cleanly paired, but he points to Krugman 2008 and to the uncredited Bernard-Eaton-Kortum priority claims. He also argues that B009's evidence quality, conceptual reach and maturity are not matched by the alternatives.
responses.response: I agree B009's foundational work is mature and that the evidence base is broad. I do not rank it below B014 on scientific grounds, and I did not in round 1. My difference with you is about bounding. For B014 the credited core is one framework, and the open questions concern who is uncredited. For B009 the open questions concern who is credited: Dorn or Katz, and whether technology and trade are one achievement or two. The chair asked what would move me to B009. A citation on which the Katz and Dorn camps agree, written explicitly as an empirical account of labour demand that does not claim the task theory, would move me substantially. Autor, Hanson and Katz would then be my preferred set. Without that, I do not think the breadth of support settles the attribution problem for me.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B009 first with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. He says my case for B014 made him more positive about it than his opening rank suggested, because Helpman's role is clear and Krugman 2008 concerned trade patterns and geography, not firm selection. He still lists B014 only as an alternative.
responses.response: Thank you. I agree with your reading of Krugman 2008. I do not take your movement as support for a configuration, since you still prefer B009, and I do not count it as evidence of merit. One point from your own round 1 bears on my reasoning. You and Krusell show that the same discovery gives two defensible trios, depending on whether the achievement is the China shock or the broader wage-structure account. That is the reason I find B014's boundary easier to state. The caution runs the other way too: your point that Helpman's candidacy is split with B049 is real, and I would draft the citation so that his credit rests only on the heterogeneous-firm and FDI work.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B045 first, with Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn as the cleanest BLP attribution. He accepts that Bresnahan's claim and the question of whether demand estimation and dynamic-industry work form one citation are open. He read my ranking of B045 third as a trade-off between honouring BLP and the broader structural-IO agenda.
responses.response: I agree with how you resolve that trade-off, and I find your argument that a methods contribution should be judged by what it changed in what can be measured persuasive. I do not apply a lower standard to B045 for being a method. Merger review and the spread of BLP into trade and other fields are real evidence of transfer. I do not make it my preferred part for two reasons. First, my familiarity with IO is exactly where I should be most careful about overweighting, and I cannot offer outside evidence on it beyond what is in the record. Second, a citation covering demand estimation and Pakes's dynamic-industry work may be two achievements. A Bresnahan-inclusive version would change the shape of the prize and not only the names. B045 stays an alternative for me, and I would support a tightly drawn BLP-only citation if the committee preferred a methods prize.

uncertainties: Whether the priority claims of Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum and Hopenhayn are strong enough that a Melitz-Helpman citation overstates the novelty of the framework, even when worded around selection and reallocation.
How much of the welfare-gain claim survives the Arkolakis-Costinot-Rodriguez-Clare critique, and whether that should affect more than the wording of the citation.
Whether the committee can define the B009 achievement and draft a citation that resolves the Dorn-or-Katz choice. That would change my assessment of B009 as the better-bounded part.
How to weigh Helpman's split candidacy under B049 against the independence of his heterogeneous-firm contribution.
Whether my own field proximity leads me to overweight firm-level trade and IO evidence relative to labour-market evidence.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to any credited name on B014, B009 or B045 is apparent from the supplied profile. For transparency, I work on exchange-rate pass-through, invoicing currency and pricing under imperfect competition, which is adjacent to B014 and B045, and I co-authored an IJIO 2026 paper with committee chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen. None of this is a link to a credited name. My spouse is a Swedish politician. This is a public fact only, and no bearing on any shortlisted achievement is apparent. These are disclosed and not adjudicated, and I claim no independent verification beyond the supplied profile.
